phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar sibilant [s] with close back vowel [u] and final [n], Tone 1 (high level, ˥). The surname Sūn 孫, "grandchild, descendant".
The bare vowel [u], Tone 4 (falling, ˥˩). Wù 悟 is "awakening, enlightenment" — the pivot syllable, and it falls like a gavel.
Voiceless unaspirated velar stop [k] with final [ʊŋ], Tone 1 (high level, ˥). Kōng 空 is "emptiness, the void" — the Buddhist technical term the whole name resolves to.

pronunciation.approximation: SOON-oo-KOHNG — first syllable high and level like a held note, middle syllable falling away sharply, last high and level again; the 'o' of kōng is like the 'oo' in 'book'.

kin.label: Self-awarded title
kin.form: 齊天大聖 Qítiān Dàshèng, "Great Sage Equal to Heaven"

kin.label: Antecedent

pronunciation.note: Sūnwùkōng is Tier 1 because the tone-marked restoration preserves a distinctive feature ASCII loses: the citation tones of all three syllables (ū, ù, ō). The name is native Chinese — sūn "grandchild", wù "awakening", kōng "emptiness", glossed in the novel itself as "Monkey awakened to emptiness" — so unlike a transcription such as Nézhā, the full Mandarin tonal reading applies, recorded in the Unihan Database (kMandarin) and standard dictionaries.

domains.title: Monkey King
domains.subtitle: Monkey King, Chaos, Enlightenment
domains.lead: Sūnwùkōng, the Monkey King, is chaos with a crown: born from stone, armed from the sea floor, appointed Great Sage Equal to Heaven by his own proclamation, and finally harnessed as the guardian of the scripture pilgrimage — the untamed mind that Buddhism learned to employ.

cards.name: The Stone Egg
cards.desc: Born from an immortal stone egg on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, nourished by sun, moon, and the essence of creation — a monkey owing nothing to any parent.

cards.name: The Compliant Gold-Banded Staff
cards.desc: The Rúyì Jīngū Bàng, a 13,500-catty iron pillar that once pinned the seas; to the Monkey King it shrinks to a needle behind the ear and grows to a pillar that props up heaven.

cards.name: Havoc in Heaven
cards.desc: Insulted with the stable-boy title Bìmǎwēn, he storms out of heaven, proclaims himself Qítiān Dàshèng, and defeats the celestial host until Laozi's furnace forges his fiery golden eyes.

cards.name: The Victorious Fighting Buddha
cards.desc: Bound to the monk Tripitaka by the golden fillet and the headache spell, he fights through eighty-one tribulations and receives the most martial of the Buddha's titles at the journey's end.

symbols.name: Rúyì Jīngū Bàng (如意金箍棒)
symbols.meaning: The compliant staff — the sea's own measure, once used to pin the floods, carried off from the East Sea treasury; a cosmic instrument reduced to a personal weapon

symbols.name: The golden fillet (緊箍兒)
symbols.meaning: The band Tripitaka tightens with a spell — the will, harnessed: the novel's whole argument that the mind's power is safe only under a vow

symbols.name: Jīndǒuyún, the cloud-somersault
symbols.meaning: 108,000 li in a single flip — the speed of an ungoverned mind, which can outrun every army and not outrun one palm

symbols.name: The fiery golden eyes (火眼金睛)
symbols.meaning: Forged in Laozi's eight-trigram furnace — eyes that see through every disguise and illusion, heaven's punishment turned into the pilgrim's greatest gift

symbols.name: The peaches and the pills
symbols.meaning: Stolen longevity — the Peaches of Immortality and Laozi's elixir pills, the wages of the Heavenly revolt, digested into a body heaven cannot process

symbols.name: Five Phases Mountain (五行山)
symbols.meaning: The Buddha's hand made landscape — five hundred years of imprisonment under a wall of stone, the weight of consequence for the wager the monkey could not imagine losing

mythology.lead: The Monkey King's story is China's great comic epic of self-mastery: born from a stone egg, tutored in the arts of immortality, at war with heaven itself — then bound to a monk and set on a road that turns the cosmic delinquent into a Buddha. Every age has read its own rebellion in him.

myths.title: Born from the Stone Egg
myths.text: The novel opens at the beginning of its world-within-a-world: on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, an immortal stone egg, left over from the creation and nourished by the essence of sun, moon, heaven, and earth, one day splits in the wind. From it steps a stone monkey, who at once bows to the four directions — and the beams of light that shoot from his golden eyes startle the Jade Emperor on his distant throne (Journey to the West, ch. 1). The new-made monkey leads his tribe through the waterfall curtain into the Water-Curtain Cave, and the discovery wins him a crown: Handsome Monkey King. He is born twice over — from stone, and from the water's test — owing nothing to any parent, court, or god. The book's whole psychology is in that birth: the Monkey King is the self-made self, and heaven will spend a hundred chapters trying to make it answerable.

myths.title: Striking Out the Names of Death
myths.text: The first grief of the Monkey King's life is an old monkey's death, and it sends him on the novel's first quest: to learn the secret of escaping mortality. For eight or nine years he wanders — across seas, through markets, in the guise of a scholar — until he reaches Mount Lingtai and the cave of the Patriarch Subodhi, who takes him as a disciple, names him Wùkōng, "Awakened to Emptiness," and teaches him the two arts that will make him famous and impossible: the seventy-two transformations and the cloud-somersault, 108,000 li in a single flip (ch. 1–2). Even death cannot keep him. When the soul-snatchers of the underworld drag him down while he sleeps, he bullies the Ten Kings of Hell, seizes the Registers of Death, and strikes out his own name and every monkey’s in the tribe (ch. 3). The episode fixes his character forever — faced with the one law no creature escapes, his answer is not repentance but erasure.

myths.title: The Great Sage Equal to Heaven
myths.text: Heaven's answer to an unmanageable genius is a job: the post of Bìmǎwēn, Protector of the Horses. When Wùkōng learns the title is stable-boy slang for a low groom, he storms out of heaven and appoints himself — with splendid insubordination — the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, the words carved on his banner (ch. 3–4). Heaven's armies cannot take him. He routs the celestial host until Erlang Shen's divine hound and Laozi's diamond snare bring him down; Laozi bakes him in the Eight-Trigram furnace for forty-nine days, which fails to kill him and instead forges his fiery golden eyes (ch. 6–7). The havoc myth made him the patron of every rebellious reader in Chinese history, and it is precisely structured: heaven's sin against him is not cruelty but condescension — and condescension, the novel says, is the one insult a true sage cannot survive.

myths.title: Buddha's Palm and the Five Phases Mountain
myths.text: At the height of the rebellion the Buddha makes a gentle, lethal offer: leap out of my right hand, and heaven is yours; fail, and return to the earth as a demon and repent. Wùkōng somersaults 108,000 li, finds five flesh-pink pillars he takes for the pillars of the world, writes his title on the middle one, and — to certify the journey — leaves a mark at its base. He leaps back, claims the throne, and the Buddha unclenches his hand: the pillars were his fingers, and the signature drips from them (ch. 7). For the wager he seals Wùkōng under Five Phases Mountain — iron pills when hungry, molten copper when thirsty — for five hundred years, until a passing monk is moved to lift the seal. The myth is the novel's hinge and its most quoted parable: the ego cannot imagine a container it did not measure. The universe, it turns out, is the one hand the monkey could not see.

myths.title: Eighty-One Tribulations
myths.text: The monk Tripitaka frees him from the mountain — and immediately binds him with the golden fillet and the headache spell, so that the most powerful creature in fiction must obey the most fragile of pilgrims (ch. 13–14). Thus conscripted, Wùkōng becomes the guardian of a journey through eighty-one tribulations: demons coveting the monk's flesh for its elixir-power, river-dragons and spider-spirits, false paradises and borrowed identities, drought demons and grieving kings — until the true scriptures are carried back from India and the pilgrims are ranked by merit (ch. 100). Wùkōng, the born rebel, receives the most martial of the Buddha's titles: Victorious Fighting Buddha (Dòuzhànshèngfó). The ending is the myth's quiet surprise. He is not defeated, disgraced, or tamed — he is employed. The cosmic delinquent did not leave the system; the system finally found the one job he was made for.

lore.syncretism: Sūnwùkōng is a palimpsest, and scholarship has mapped his layers. At the bottom lies the historical pilgrimage: the monk Xuánzàng's journey to India (629–645 CE) and its biography, the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions. Over it the storytellers laid a monkey-disciple motif that appears by the Song in the Poetic Tale of Tripitaka's Pilgrimage and in the Yuan-Ming zaju play attributed to Yang Jingxian — and beneath that, some argue, the Tang tale of the water-monster Wuzhiqi, chained by Yu the Great (Li Gongzuo, Guwuyue jing). The Indian Hanuman has been proposed as a source since the twentieth century; the case is suggestive but contested, and most scholarship now treats Wùkōng as a largely indigenous synthesis dressed in Buddhist pilgrimage clothes. Daoist readers then recast the whole novel as inner alchemy: Wùkōng is the xīnyuán, the monkey of the mind, whose harnessing is the work of cultivation. The figure travelled onward as Son Goku in Japan, Tôn Ngộ Không in Vietnam, and Seoyugi's pilgrim in Korea.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Monkey King is arguably the most retold character in Chinese history. The 1592 Shidetang edition fixed the novel; Peking opera made havoc-in-heaven a signature sequence; the 1986 CCTV television series became one of the most-watched dramas ever aired in the Chinese-speaking world, rebroadcast every summer since. The diaspora carried him into global pop culture — Japan's Son Goku, and through it the Dragon Ball franchise — and the 2024 video game Black Myth: Wukong carried him to the top of world sales charts, a Ming-dynasty pilgrim headlining a global entertainment industry. Meanwhile he never ceased to be a god: the cult of Qítiān Dàshèng persists in Fujian and Taiwan, where his temples, mediums, and festival troupes treat the Great Sage as a living, oath-binding power. The rebel has two afterlives, and neither cancels the other.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Wùkōng is the mind itself, and every reader of the novel eventually notices the allegory hiding in plain sight. Chan literature had long called the restless spirit the "monkey of the mind" (xīnyuán) — the faculty that somersaults from thought to thought faster than any storm, sees through every disguise, and cannot sit still inside even the walls of heaven. The novel gives that monkey a body, a weapon, and a résumé, then asks the only question that matters: what finally disciplines him? Not the armies of heaven, not the furnace of Laozi, not five hundred years under a mountain. A vow — freely accepted, and administered by the weakest person on the road.

That is why the story never goes stale. Every age has its own Wùkōng: the prodigy too gifted for the institution, the startup too unruly for the regulator, the talent the system first insults and then needs. And every age gets the same ending — not the destruction of the monkey, which would be a loss, but his employment, which is a redemption. The five phases mountain becomes a pilgrimage. The hand that beats him also frees him. The mind, fully employed, is a Buddha.

lore.archaeology: Wùkōng's material record tracks the novel's. The earliest narrative stratum is the Song Poetic Tale of Tripitaka's Pilgrimage; the Ming zaju play was preserved in part through the Yongle Encyclopedia; and the 1592 Shidetang woodblock edition of Journey to the West is the earliest extant complete text. The cult beneath the literature is older than the novel: a Song-dated stone shrine at Baoshan, Shunchang County, Fujian, dedicated to Qítiān Dàshèng and his brother Tōngtiān Dàshèng, is among the earliest material evidence of the Great Sage's worship — decades, at least, before the novel fixed his story. Qítiān Dàshèng temples remain active across Fujian and Taiwan, where the Great Sage's spirit-medium rites are among the most dramatic survivals of Chinese popular religion.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 孫悟空 in traditional Chinese, 孙悟空 simplified. Sūn 孫 is the surname ("grandchild, descendant"); wù 悟 is "awakening, enlightenment"; kōng 空 is "emptiness, the void" — the Buddhist technical term. The novel glosses the full name as the monkey awakened to emptiness. The tone-marked restoration Sūnwùkōng keeps all three citation tones (sūn Tone 1, wù Tone 4, kōng Tone 1); no apostrophe is needed, as the segmentation sūn·wù·kōng is unambiguous.
